messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa's eyes go to the clerk's desk and stay there a moment, the capped inkwell, the stool pushed square, before she turns back to Vell.

"Before we go, I have three questions, Master Vell. Who has been into Jassan's room since he died? The landlord, the watch, anyone from this house? A room that's been searched once is easier to take things from than one nobody has touched."

She taps the counter once, where his finger had been.

"Second, the seal. What is pressed into it, and whose wax is it? If we have to swear to you that it arrived whole, I want to know what we are swearing to."

Her voice softens a little. "And third: does anyone else know you've sent for this box? A man who has lost his clerk and a strongbox in one week is a man people come asking after."

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell leans on the counter's edge, eyes going once to the tidy desk and back to Vell.

"Three questions, Master Vell, and then we're off. Who found Ferr, and who's been up those stairs since? A room that's been looked over by the wrong people is a room with the seal half-broken before we reach it. What's the seal like? Wax, ribbon, your own mark? I want to know what whole looks like before I'm the one who has to say it isn't. And the lock. Key or combination? Did Ferr keep his key on him, or did you have to take it off the body?"

He glances at Sefa and Bram before he speaks again. "I'll not be paying for a broken box, Vell."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I wait until Vell stops tapping the counter, then look past him at the clerk's desk with its pushed-in stool.

"Three things," I say. "How big is the box, and what does it weigh? If it's iron-banded oak, we'll want a handcart, not three pairs of arms. Second, who has the key? Ferr's, or yours? And third, who's been up in that room since Ferr died? The cooper, the Watch, anyone with a reason to look?"

I tip my head toward the desk. "Somebody tidied that before they sent for us. I'd like to know who, and whether they took anything with them."

Vell's mouth tightens at the mention of the stairs. He answers without looking at the desk.

"Wenna Pike keeps the house above Tobin's yard. She found him, three mornings back, and sent her boy for the Watch. A Watch clerk went up once, the same day, and wrote down that he was dead. Then the physician from the Song of the Morning. Nobody else that I know of. I haven't set foot on those stairs." He pauses. "Wenna has the room key. She has been very clear that she wants her rent."

To Pell: "Wax. Dark green, pressed with the scales. My house's mark. It was whole when the box came to me, and I didn't look at it closer than that." His finger stops on the counter. "The box has its own lock. A key, not a combination. Jassan wore the key on a cord at his neck. The cord went to Wenna with his coat. Ask her for it."

To Bram: "Oak, banded with iron, about the length of my forearm. Heavy. The cooper's boy and I carried it up to his room the week he took the place, and I was sorry for it by the top step." He glances at the desk for the first time and away again. "I didn't touch that desk. Jassan kept it so. Whether Wenna or the Watch straightened it after, I couldn't tell you."

He looks from one of them to the next. "Who knows I sent for it? My clerk is dead. I told no one but the three of you, and the people you're going to ask for keys." He does not say the other name he might have said. "Go before the light changes. Bring it here whole."

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell doesn't look at the desk for long. He's already counting the cooper's yard in his head.

"Good. Now the one that matters to me. Above Tobin's yard, is there a window on the back wall, or a balcony over the barrels? Roofs don't care about the Watch's stairs." He glances at Sefa and Bram, then back at Vell. "I'll go to Wenna Pike for the key and the cord. You two can keep her talking at the front door, and I'll see what the room looks like before anyone's feet go in. Anyone who went up there before us will have left some sign, and I'd rather find it than be told about it."

He leans in a little, voice dropping. "And Master Vell, if Ferr kept a ledger he didn't want the Watch reading, he'd have kept it close. Did he have a habit of hiding things, or a friend who might know where?"

He straightens, hand already on the counter's edge ready to go. "Also, the moment you're carrying that box out of here, don't stop to admire the seal. Somebody will be watching the door."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I nod at Vell's answers and turn to the others.

"Wenna first, then the stairs. Sefa, you've the kind voice for a landlady who wants her rent paid. Pell, if the key's not on the body, it's on her. Let her see we mean to pay, and she'll tell us what she moved." I look back at Vell. "What's the Watch clerk's name? If his notes say how Ferr lay and what was on the table, I want them before I've touched a thing."

I rest my hand on the counter, near the ledger nearest the desk, and keep my eyes on the stool. "And Vell, leave that desk as it is. Nobody moves that stool until we've seen the room."

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa lets Vell finish, then looks at the stool under the clerk's desk, pushed in so square it might have been measured.

"Thank you, Master Vell. One thing more, and then we'll go." She keeps her voice low and even. "You said you told no one but us. I believe you. But you were quick to say it, and a man who is quick to say a thing is often thinking of someone else. Did Jassan have a sister, a friend, a debt-holder who would have asked where he was?"

She turns to Pell and Bram without waiting for the answer. "Wenna Pike wants her rent and has the key. I'll take her. A landlady who has been asked for rent by a stranger all week will talk more readily to a woman who asks after her health and her grandchildren. Pell, the Watch clerk who went up the first day; find out what he wrote down and whether he took anything with him. Bram, go with Pell up to the room if she'll unlock it, and see who else has used those stairs. I'd like the physician's name before we leave the yard, too, if anyone can tell me where the Song of the Morning keeps its healers this week."

She looks at the desk once more, then at Vell. "And Master Vell, if the seal is whole when we bring it, I'd like to see it before it goes in your hands. Not because I doubt you. Because the next person to ask about that box will want to know who looked first."

scenes.narration:
Vell answers without lifting his eyes from the scales. "A window on the back wall, over the yard. A shutter, no glass. The wash-house roof runs under it, slate, and Tobin's barrels are stacked beneath. No balcony. The stair comes up inside the house to a door on the landing, and that is the only way in that I know of." He sets the weight down. "I went up once, the week he took the place. I didn't stay."

To Sefa: "A sister in Nashkel, he said once. He never said her name, and no one came asking for him here but the Watch." To Pell: "He kept his drawers locked and his letters went out from that desk. Whether he hid anything, I couldn't tell you. I never looked in his drawers. That was what I paid him for." To Bram: "A Watch clerk. Young, with a cold in him, I thought. He didn't give his name and I didn't ask it." He looks at the stool for the first time since the start, and then at the door. "Who tidied that desk, I don't know. Not me."

Pell is already at the door, one hand on the frame. He nods to the other two and goes out first, into the hammering, and the street takes him the way a street takes a man who does not want to be looked at. The Coast Way runs south out of the town past the smithies, the cart ruts still wet from the night's rain. Tobin's yard sits back from the road behind a gate of split oak, barrels stacked in rows along its wall, the sour smell of wet staves coming over the top.

On the left-hand gatepost, at the height of a man's shoulder, someone has drawn a small chalk ring with a line through it and a notch cut in the line. Pell knows it at once. He has seen that mark on a hundred doors in the Lower City, and it means what it always meant: someone is watching this house, and someone is paid to. He does not stop. He does not touch it. He turns his shoulder to the gate and goes along the wall as if he were only looking for the lane behind.

Sefa and Bram walk up to the front door of the house. The boy on the step gets up and goes in without being asked. A moment later the door opens and a woman comes out wiping her hands on her apron, a key already in her fist, a cord hanging from it that she has not yet let swing. She looks at the two of them, then at the yard gate, where Pell's back has just passed out of sight behind the barrels.

"You're Vell's," she says. "I was told three." Her eyes go to Bram's shield and stay there a moment. "Ferr owed me three gold and four silver, and nobody goes up my stairs till it's paid. Rent first, then the key. That's how I've done it all week, and it hasn't changed for the Watch or for Vell." She holds the key a little higher, the cord swinging loose. "So. Which of you has the coin?"

messages.text:
Sefa steps forward, close enough that Wenna can see she isn't reaching for a weapon, and smiles as if the rent were the most reasonable thing in the world.

"Three gold and four silver. That's fair, and I'll not haggle a landlady over money she's owed." She opens her purse, counts out three gold and four silver into her palm, and holds it out. "I'm paying it from my own purse, mind. Master Vell will settle with me afterward, and I'd rather not argue with him about it today."

She keeps the coins in her hand a moment longer, so Wenna has to look at her to take them.

"How is your back this week, Mistress Pike? The stairs in a house like this must be hard on you. And the little one on the step, is that your grandson? He's a quick one, I could see it from the road."

Her voice stays easy, but she is listening for anything Wenna doesn't say.

"Now, I'll take the key, and the cord with it, since Jassan wore them and his things should go to the people who'll see them rightly used. Before I go up, though, I'd like to know who else has climbed those stairs since the Watch came. Not the clerk, I know about him. Anyone who came asking, or came to take something, or who you've turned away."

scenes.narration:
Wenna's hand closes over the coins Sefa holds out. She counts them without looking down, the way a woman counts who has taken rent for years. Bram's hand is still open with three silver pieces in it. She glances at them and shakes her head. "One payment's enough. I've had mine." He tips the silver back into his pouch.

"So." She tucks the coins into her apron pocket. "My back's the same, thank you. Tam's my grandson, and he'll be a thief if nobody stops him, so you're right about the quick." She looks at Sefa a moment longer than she needs to, then holds up the key and the cord it hangs from. "Jassan's. The key's for the room door. The little brass one on the cord is for his box, I'd think. He never let it off his neck."

She puts both into Sefa's palm and does not let go of the cord until Sefa has her fingers round it.

"The Watch boy came first, the morning I found him. The one with the cold in his nose. He went up, wrote in a book on the landing, came down and sneezed into my yard. He took nothing out that I saw, and I stood at the foot of the stair the whole time." She folds her arms. "Then the physician from the Song of the Morning, the second day. Looked, said it was what you'd expect with a man of his build, and went down."

She shifts her weight, and her eyes go past them to the yard gate.

"And a quiet man in a grey coat came round twice. From a counting-house on the Trade Way, he said, though he didn't say which. He wanted to know what was in the room, and he had an open purse and offered me more than the rent for it. I told him to ask the Watch." Her mouth tightens. "He didn't care for that."

To Bram, flatly: "The desk? I never touched his papers. I went up the once, to see him, and came straight down. Whoever put that stool square, it wasn't me." She looks at him as if he were the one who should explain it. "Door's been shut since. I've had the key in my apron. Nobody's gone in but the Watch, and they went in with my boy holding the lamp."

She steps back from the step and lets the boy on it slide past her into the house, then looks at Sefa again.

"Up you go. The door sticks at the top. Lift it, don't shove it." At the last, dryly, as she turns to her yard: "And Master Vell can settle his own accounts with you. I've had mine."

 No roll was needed: each of these was already told in the story above, and none is a contest. Sefa's payment and key, her questions and Wenna's answers were routine dealings, and Bram's second payment was refused by Wenna herself.

Pell crosses the wall as if the lane were empty. The shutter on the back wall is a plank frame with no glass, latched on the inside by a bar that drops into an iron keeper. Pell sets his fingers on the sill and looks at the keeper before he touches anything. The bar sits square, but the wood round the keeper is pale and fresh, with a thin bright scrape where something narrow has been worked under the bar and lifted. The scrape is not three days old. Dust from the slates has settled over the rest of the sill, and it has not settled over that.

Below him the yard is quiet. The barrels creak once in the wind and are still.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I fold Odda Brand's letter small and push it into my belt pouch, under the coins. Neither of the others sees it, and I keep my face where it was.

Sefa has the key and the brass cord. I put a hand on the door frame and say, low enough that Wenna won't hear over the yard, "Up we go, and I go first. Keep your voice down." The stairs are steep and narrow, with a turn at the top. I take them one step at a time and check each tread for scuffs, a smear of wet, anything that doesn't look like a cooper's dust. I've walked enough wagon ramps to read the wood.

At the landing I stop and look back at the door. Wenna's voice drifts up from the yard, pitched to carry, telling the boy to fetch the water.

"Sefa," I say. "Before you put that key in, tell me what you make of the quiet man in the grey coat. Counting-house on the Trade Way, open purse, and Wenna sent him off to the Watch. A man who wants the room that badly doesn't go away after one refusal. And somebody tidied that desk before Vell sent for us. I'd like to know who else has been standing in that room."

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa tucks the cord into her palm, the little brass key warm from Wenna's hand, and nods to the old woman as if they had agreed on everything.

"Thank you, Mistress Pike. Your back is in good hands with the boy, I think." She turns to Bram. "Come up with me. Stand at the top of the stairs, where you can see the landing and the street door both. If anyone climbs after us, I want to hear it before they reach the door."

At the top she lifts the door as Wenna told her, and it comes free without a sound. The room is cold and smells of lamp oil and damp wool. A narrow bed is made up square. A table holds an empty cup, a pen, and a stack of paper weighted with a stone. The shutter on the back wall is closed, and a grey thread of light comes around its edge.

Before she goes in, Sefa stops on the landing where the Watch clerk's book lies open on a shelf by the door. She runs one finger down the page without touching the ink, reading the cramped hand.

"'Third day of the month, morning. Jassan Ferr, clerk, found dead in bed. No wound. Face dark, as if from strangling or a fit. Door locked from within. Key with the landlady. Nothing taken that is known.'" She frowns. "Then a second line, added after, in a different ink: 'Strongbox noted, not opened, not removed.' There's no name under it. Only the Watch's stamp, and the stamp is smudged."

She straightens and looks at Bram. "Nothing taken that is known. Someone wrote that line knowing it might be untrue. Keep your eyes on that door."

Then she turns to the room, and her gaze goes straight to the floor by the bed, where the boards are a shade paler in a square the size of a strongbox.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell lies still on the slate for a breath, then reaches for the sill without letting his weight shift the tiles.

"Someone's been in," he says under his breath, and it is not a question. He thumbs the pale scrape, then sights along the bar from the side, mouth tight. "Thin blade, worked under and lifted. Not a Watch man's crowbar. Someone who knew how to open a shutter without leaving a mess." He leans closer, eyes on the iron keeper. "Lifted once, set back. Sloppy with the wood, neat with the bar. Could be the same hand that sent the watcher to the cart, or just somebody who came before us and didn't want the landlady to know."

He draws his dagger slowly, not to use it, just to hold the point of it under the bar and test the lift without moving the latch. "I'm not going through the shutter yet. The bar's been set, so whoever lifted it set it for a reason. I'll see if it moves for me the same way before I put my weight on it."

He glances down at the yard, then toward the street where Sefa's voice would be, though he can't hear it from here. "Sefa, Wenna's door. I've got a window that's been opened by someone who isn't Wenna. Tell me what she says about the stairs."

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa answers Bram without turning from the bed. "The grey coat wants the box, and he has money to get it. A man who offers more than the rent for a room hasn't finished with the room. He'll come back, and not by the front door." She glances toward the top of the stairs. "And I think someone who wasn't Wenna or the Watch straightened that desk. The tidying was done by someone who knew Jassan kept his papers in order, and knew Vell wouldn't look. Keep your shield where it is. If the stair creaks, call me."

She kneels on the boards beside the bed, careful not to lean her weight on the pale rectangle, and looks at the wax without touching it. The Rune Keeper's gift lets her read what is pressed there. The scales are plain, Vell's house mark. Beside them, smaller and pressed deeper, is a second stamp: a half-moon with a line drawn through it, and under the line, in letters no bigger than a grain of rice, two words in Common. *Paid. Sealed.*

Her breath stops for a moment. She knows the half-moon from nowhere she can name, but she knows what *paid* means on a box that was never Vell's to send. Whoever sealed this strongbox was not a moneylender's clerk. They were telling someone the job was finished.

Sefa does not break the seal. She stays on her knees, takes the candle from her pack, and lights it from the tinderbox, shading the flame with her hand so that the light falls on the wax and nothing else.

"Bram," she says quietly, "come and look at this before you say anything about the box. The seal isn't only Vell's. And I don't think Jassan's landlady was the last person to stand in this room."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I keep my back to the wall and my eyes on the stairwell. The shield stays between me and the way down.

"Call it out as you go, Sefa," I say, low. "The box, the lock, the seal, and whether anything's been scraped or pried. And take a look at the window too. Pell's going to come up from the yard side, and I'd rather not guess which way he'll be climbing."

I keep my voice down so it carries no further than the door. "On the grey coat: one man who wants a room badly enough to offer more than the rent, a clerk's desk squared up by somebody nobody will name, and a dead man's strongbox that Vell can't stop talking around. Whoever tidied that desk was in here before the Watch wrote their line in the book, or they'd not have bothered. Keep that in mind when you touch the lock."

I don't look at the door to Jassan's room. I watch the stairwell and the street below through the gap at the turn, and I listen for boots on the steps.

presses.text:
Sefa holds the flame where it is and looks until her eyes sting. The grain under the wax keeps its shape, and the closed eye stays closed. Whatever lies beneath is too fine and too deep for her to read by one candle. She can feel that it is something made to be read by someone, and that she is not that someone yet.

The warmth in her palms climbs, then settles. The voice does not come again. What comes instead is a simple certainty, like the Lantern's light on a page: this is not a clerk's seal, and it was not meant to be broken by a clerk's hand.

She lifts the candle away from the wax and sets it on the boards, well clear of the pale rectangle.

"I can't read it," she says to Bram, very low. "Not in this light, and I won't break the seal to find out. But I can tell you it isn't Vell's mark that matters. The eye is the mark of whoever sealed this, and it was sealed to say the job was finished, and they didn't want the box opened on the way to Vell." She glances at the window shutter, where the grey light comes around the edge. "Pell is in the yard, or he should be. If anyone comes up the wall or along the wash-house roof, that's our way in and out. Keep watching the stairs."

She does not reach for the box yet.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell waits a breath longer, watching the watcher's back at the lane's end, then sets the dagger's point under the bar again.

"Sefa's at the door, and that man's got his eyes on her, not on the roof," he murmurs. "I'm going in now, while the stairs are still a long way off."

He lifts the bar the way it was lifted before, one finger's width, and slides the shutter back just enough to fit his body through. He drops feet first onto the boards inside, crouches under the sill, and waits for the house to answer. Nothing but the drip of the wash-house gutter outside.

Before he stands, his eyes go over the floor: the dust by the door, the bed, the oak box with its iron bands. He keeps his boots off the one clean stretch in front of the box. Then he looks for the drawers Vell mentioned, locked, and for anyone else's tracks in the grey dust.

"Two sets of boot-marks on the floor," he whispers to himself. "One fresh, one older. The fresh one stops at the box and turns back."

cards.title: Investigation: reading the boot-marks in the dust of Jassan's room, which are fresh and which are old

presses.text:
The grey dust has kept a clear record. Three days of undisturbed dust lie over most of the floor, and the older marks are Jassan's own: a clerk's plain soft shoes, worn at the heel, going from the bed to the desk and back a hundred times, with a patch where he always stood.

Over those marks run newer ones. A heavier boot, a man's by the size of it, with a square toe and a nail missing from the sole. These prints are sharp at the edges, and the dust has not yet filled them in. They come in from the door and go straight to the oak box. The dust around it is pressed in two places, where a man knelt and then pushed back on his heels. Then the prints turn and go to the desk. Here they wander. The drawers have been tried: a fingernail's worth of scoring around the lock of the lowest one, and a pale wedge of wood where something was levered and slipped. After that the prints go back to the door and out onto the landing.

There is a third mark, close to the bed, that you can't put a foot to: a long smear in the dust, as if a sack or a bundle had been dragged a short way and then lifted.

The box itself has no marks on its lid. The wax seal on its clasp is whole, dark green, pressed with the scales. Nobody has broken it.

From the landing, very faintly, you hear the house stir: a door, feet on the stairs, a woman's voice raised in the street. The sound is Sefa's, speaking to Wenna Pike, and it is coming up the stairwell toward the room.

Pell freezes at the sound of Sefa's voice on the stairs, then sees that the print under the shutter is his own. He notes it and keeps still.

"That's mine," he breathes, and hooks a boot toe over the edge of the sill so no more dust gets stirred. "The narrow ones with no nails, from the door to the bed and back. Those are the ones I want."

He keeps to the far side of the old marks, moving only as far as the box, and looks at the oak lid without touching it. The green wax is whole, the scales pressed sharp. He does not lift the box, only tilts his head to see the clasp and the lock plate. A key, as Vell said, and no scratches around it.

"Lock's not been worked," he murmurs. "Whoever came first didn't want the box. They wanted the drawers."

He eases toward the desk, keeping his boots out of the clean rectangle beside the bed, and looks at the drawer where a wedge of pale wood shows. He does not try the lock. Downstairs, Wenna's voice rises, and Sefa's answers, calm and soft.

"Sefa's bringing her up," he says, quieter. "Bram, if you're listening through that door, stand where the landing light doesn't reach the box. I want to be behind the bed when that latch goes."

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
"Whole," Sefa says, low and steady. "The pressing is sharp. Vell's scales are there, dark green, and there's no ribbon, only the wax itself. Under the scales is the eye, and the eye is pressed deeper than the scales. Nothing's cracked and nothing's lifted."

She keeps her eyes on the wax a moment longer, then looks at the stair gap. "The man in the brown jerkin. Is he watching the front door, or the yard gate? If he's looking at the house, he's looking at the wrong window. Tell me if he moves toward the wash-house wall."

She does not touch the lock. Instead she lays two fingers flat on the iron band nearest her and rocks the box a fraction, testing its weight against the floor. It shifts without a sound. Whatever is inside is heavy, and it sits still.

"I won't open it here," she says. "Vell wants it whole, and so do the people who sealed it. Pell's the one who knows how to get a box down a wall without being seen." She turns toward the shutter, cups one hand beside her mouth, and speaks through the gap in a voice no louder than a draught: "Pell. Back wall. The box is here, and we need a way down that doesn't go past the front door."

Then she looks back at the cord in her palm and the brass key on it, and does not put it to the lock yet.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I keep the shield across the gap and don't take my eyes off the lane. The grey coat is out of sight now, but the brown jerkin is still on his cart.

"Sefa, the wax," I say quietly. "Is the seal whole? If anyone's been at it, I'd rather know before Vell does."

I shift my boots on the top step so I can hear the stairwell below, and I wait.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell eases back along the far wall, away from the clean rectangle, and slides in behind the narrow bed where the shadow is deepest. He crouches low, one hand flat on the boards, the other resting on the hilt of his shortsword.

"Stairs first, then the latch," he breathes toward the door. "Sefa, keep her in the doorway. Don't let her walk past the box. If she's seen the box, she'll wonder why we're looking at the drawers."

He glances once at the desk, at the pale wedge in the wood beside the lock, and files it away. Nothing else will be touched until the landlady has said her piece.

"Bram, when the door opens, you stay where the light doesn't reach. I'll be out of her eye by the bed." He pauses, listening to Wenna's voice climb the last steps. "And if she asks who's been up here before us, let her say it first. Landladies always know more than they mean to tell."

Where you are: Ostrin Vell's counting-house, at the long counter · Time: Day 1 · morning

Sefa's gaze settles on the clerk's desk for a moment before she turns back to Vell. She says she has three questions. First, who has entered Jassan's room since his death, whether landlord, Watch or anyone from the house, because a room already searched once is easier to rob. Second, what is pressed into the seal and whose wax it is, so that she knows what they would be swearing to. Third, whether anyone besides Vell knows he sent for the box, since a man who has lost a clerk and a strongbox in one week gets people asking after him. She taps the counter where his finger had been. Pell, leaning on the counter's edge, glances at the desk and says that he too has three questions and then they are off. He asks who found Ferr and who has climbed the stairs since, what the seal looks like, whether wax, ribbon or Vell's own mark, and whether the lock takes a key or a combination, and whether Ferr's key was taken off the body. He says he won't pay for a broken box.

Vell's mouth tightens at the mention of the stairs. He answers without looking at the desk.

"Wenna Pike keeps the house above Tobin's yard. She found him three mornings back and sent her boy for the Watch. A Watch clerk went up once, the same day, and wrote down that he was dead. Then the physician from the Song of the Morning. Nobody else that I know of. I haven't set foot on those stairs." He pauses. "Wenna has the room key. She has been very clear that she wants her rent."

To Pell he says the wax is dark green, pressed with the scales, his house's mark. "It was whole when the box came to me, and I didn't look at it closer than that." His finger stops on the counter. The box has its own lock, a key and not a combination. Jassan wore the key on a cord at his neck, and the cord went to Wenna with his coat. "Ask her for it."

To you he says: "Oak, banded with iron, about the length of my forearm. Heavy. The cooper's boy and I carried it up to his room the week he took the place, and I was sorry for it by the top step." He glances at the desk for the first time and away again. "I didn't touch that desk. Jassan kept it so. Whether Wenna or the Watch straightened it after, I couldn't tell you."

He looks from one of you to the next. "Who knows I sent for it? My clerk is dead. I told no one but the three of you, and the people you're going to ask for keys." He does not say any other name. "Go before the light changes. Bring it here whole."

Where you are: at the counter in Vell's office · Time: Day 1 · morning

You told the others that Wenna came first and then the stairs. You asked Vell for the Watch clerk's name, and told him to leave the desk alone and not to move the stool.

Pell asked Vell whether the back wall above Tobin's yard had a window or balcony, and said he would fetch the key and the cord from Wenna Pike himself while you and Sefa kept her busy at the front door. He asked whether Ferr was in the habit of hiding things, or had a friend who might know where he kept them, and warned that whoever carried the box out should not stop to admire the seal, because someone would be watching the door.

Sefa asked Vell whether Jassan had a sister, a friend or a debt-holder who would have asked after him, noting that he had been quick to say he'd told no one. She said she would take Wenna herself, sent Pell after the Watch clerk's notes, and asked you to go up with Pell and see who else had used the stairs. She wanted the physician's name too, and wanted to see the seal whole before the box went into Vell's hands.

Vell answered Pell: a window on the back wall over the yard, a shutter with no glass. The slate wash-house roof runs under it and Tobin's barrels are stacked beneath. No balcony. The stair comes up inside the house to a door on the landing, the only way in he knows. He went up once and didn't stay. To Sefa he said Ferr once mentioned a sister in Nashkel, never named, and that no one but the Watch had come asking. Ferr kept his drawers locked, and Vell never looked in them. To you he said the clerk was young, with a cold, and gave no name. Looking at the stool for the first time, he said he didn't know who tidied that desk, and that it wasn't him.

Pell went out first and the street took him. The Coast Way runs south past the smithies, the ruts still wet from the night's rain. Tobin's yard sits back behind a gate of split oak, barrels stacked along its wall, the smell of wet staves coming over the top.

You and Sefa walk up to the front door of the house. The boy on the step gets up and goes in without being asked. A moment later a woman comes out wiping her hands on her apron, a key already in her fist and a cord hanging from it. She looks at the two of you, then at the yard gate, where Pell's back has just passed out of sight behind the barrels.

"You're Vell's," she says. "I was told three." Her eyes go to your shield and stay a moment. "Ferr owed me three gold and four silver, and nobody goes up my stairs till it's paid. Rent first, then the key. That's how I've done it all week, and it hasn't changed for the Watch or for Vell." She holds the key higher, the cord swinging loose. "So. Which of you has the coin?"

Your journal, new:
+ Goal: Vell's strongbox
+ Quest: Vell's strongbox

Where you are: at the front door of Wenna Pike's house · Time: Day 1 · morning

Beside you, Sefa stepped close to Wenna with no weapon in reach and paid the rent, three gold and four silver, from her own purse, saying Master Vell would settle with her later. She kept the coins held out so Wenna had to look at her, asked after Wenna's back and the child on the step, and asked for the key and the cord with it. Then she asked who else had climbed the stairs since the Watch came, anyone who came asking, came to take something, or was turned away.

Wenna's hand closes over the coins Sefa holds out. She counts them without looking down, the way a woman counts who has taken rent for years. Your hand is still open with three silver pieces in it. She glances at them and shakes her head. "One payment's enough. I've had mine." You tip the silver back into your pouch.

"So." She tucks the coins into her apron pocket. "My back's the same, thank you. Tam's my grandson, and he'll be a thief if nobody stops him, so you're right about the quick." She looks at Sefa a moment longer than she needs to, then holds up the key and the cord it hangs from. "Jassan's. The key's for the room door. The little brass one on the cord is for his box, I'd think. He never let it off his neck."

She puts both into Sefa's palm and does not let go of the cord until Sefa has her fingers round it.

"The Watch boy came first, the morning I found him. The one with the cold in his nose. He went up, wrote in a book on the landing, came down and sneezed into my yard. He took nothing out that I saw, and I stood at the foot of the stair the whole time." She folds her arms. "Then the physician from the Song of the Morning, the second day. Looked, said it was what you'd expect with a man of his build, and went down."

She shifts her weight, and her eyes go past you to the yard gate.

"And a quiet man in a grey coat came round twice. From a counting-house on the Trade Way, he said, though he didn't say which. He wanted to know what was in the room, and he had an open purse and offered me more than the rent for it. I told him to ask the Watch." Her mouth tightens. "He didn't care for that."

To you, flatly: "The desk? I never touched his papers. I went up the once, to see him, and came straight down. Whoever put that stool square, it wasn't me." She looks at you as if you should be the one to explain it. "Door's been shut since. I've had the key in my apron. Nobody's gone in but the Watch, and they went in with my boy holding the lamp."

She steps back from the step and lets the boy on it slide past her into the house, then looks at Sefa again.

"Up you go. The door sticks at the top. Lift it, don't shove it." At the last, dryly, as she turns to her yard: "And Master Vell can settle his own accounts with you. I've had mine."

(While the others were looking elsewhere, a boy pressed a sealed letter into your hand and was gone before anyone else saw. It is for you alone. You break the seal and read:)

«Bram — Harl died owing Ostrin Vell forty gold, and Vell's note for it is in his dead clerk's strongbox — the one Vell has hired you to bring him. Jassan wrote to me before he died: once the box is back, Vell calls the note and takes the house. If that one page were gone before Vell opened the box, there would be nothing to call. Please. I have no one else to ask. — Odda Brand»

Where you are: Wenna's yard, at the house door · Time: Day 1 · morning

Sefa takes the brass cord and key from Wenna with thanks, and says the boy will be good for the old woman's back. I wait until Vell stops tapping the counter, then look past him at the clerk's desk with its pushed-in stool.

"Three things," I say. "How big is the box, and what does it weigh? If it's iron-banded oak, we'll want a handcart, not three pairs of arms. Second, who has the key? Ferr's, or yours? And third, who's been up in that room since Ferr died? The cooper, the Watch, anyone with a reason to look?"

I tip my head toward the desk. "Somebody tidied that before they sent for us. I'd like to know who, and whether they took anything with them."

I nod at Vell's answers and turn to the others.

"Wenna first, then the stairs. Sefa, you've the kind voice for a landlady who wants her rent paid. Pell, if the key's not on the body, it's on her. Let her see we mean to pay, and she'll tell us what she moved." I look back at Vell. "What's the Watch clerk's name? If his notes say how Ferr lay and what was on the table, I want them before I've touched a thing."

I rest my hand on the counter, near the ledger nearest the desk, and keep my eyes on the stool. "And Vell, leave that desk as it is. Nobody moves that stool until we've seen the room."

"I've got the coin," I say, and reach into my belt pouch. I count out three gold and four silver into her palm, one piece at a time so she sees every one. "Ferr's debt, paid by Vell's hired hands. It comes off our fee, not off the clerk's estate, so you're not out a copper for having been patient."

I keep my hand near the pouch and my eyes on the key. "Now, Wenna. Who has been up those stairs since the Watch left? I don't mean the cooper's boy or the physician. I mean anyone who came with their own key, or who had no business there and went up anyway. And did anyone move his things before the Watch got there, or after?"

I fold Odda Brand's letter small and push it into my belt pouch, under the coins. Neither of the others sees it, and I keep my face where it was.

Sefa has the key and the brass cord. I put a hand on the door frame and say, low enough that Wenna won't hear over the yard, "Up we go, and I go first. Keep your voice down." The stairs are steep and narrow, with a turn at the top. I take them one step at a time and check each tread for scuffs, a smear of wet, anything that doesn't look like a cooper's dust. I've walked enough wagon ramps to read the wood.

At the landing I stop and look back at the door. Wenna's voice drifts up from the yard, pitched to carry, telling the boy to fetch the water.

"Sefa," I say. "Before you put that key in, tell me what you make of the quiet man in the grey coat. Counting-house on the Trade Way, open purse, and Wenna sent him off to the Watch. A man who wants the room that badly doesn't go away after one refusal. And somebody tidied that desk before Vell sent for us. I'd like to know who else has been standing in that room."

I keep my back to the wall and my eyes on the stairwell. The shield stays between me and the way down.

"Call it out as you go, Sefa," I say, low. "The box, the lock, the seal, and whether anything's been scraped or pried. And take a look at the window too. Pell's going to come up from the yard side, and I'd rather not guess which way he'll be climbing."

I keep my voice down so it carries no further than the door. "On the grey coat: one man who wants a room badly enough to offer more than the rent, a clerk's desk squared up by somebody nobody will name, and a dead man's strongbox that Vell can't stop talking around. Whoever tidied that desk was in here before the Watch wrote their line in the book, or they'd not have bothered. Keep that in mind when you touch the lock."

I don't look at the door to Jassan's room. I watch the stairwell and the street below through the gap at the turn, and I listen for boots on the steps.

I stay where I am, shield up, eyes on the turn of the stair and the lane beyond the gap. I keep my voice low.

"Sefa, what do you see on the wax?" I say. "Is it whole, and is the pressing sharp? Vell said dark green and the scales. Check the ribbon too, if there is one."

Then, quieter: "And that man in the brown jerkin. He's been by the ditch a while with an apple and nothing to do. I don't like a man with nothing to do who doesn't look at the house."

I shift my weight so the shield covers the gap, and I keep one hand on the hilt of the longsword without drawing it.

The session begins.

Beregost wakes to hammers. From every smithy along the street the ringing comes through the shutters of Ostrin Vell's counting-house, where the morning light falls on brass scales and rows of bound ledgers. You stand at the long counter with Pell Dunmore and Bram Halloway. The three of you met here only this morning, and Vell has just hired you together.

Vell lays the terms out a second time, tapping the counter with one finger at each point. Jassan Ferr, his clerk, died three days ago in a rented room above the cooper's yard on the Coast Way. In that room is a locked strongbox of ledgers. Vell wants it here before nightfall today, unopened, with its seal whole. On delivery he will pay seventy-five gold for the three of you to share. Not a copper before.

Beside the counter stands a clerk's desk. Its stool is pushed neatly under it, the inkwell is capped and the blotter is clean, as if someone had tidied it and no one had sat there since. Vell does not look at it. He looks from you to Pell to Bram, folds his hands on the counter and waits. "The Coast Way is not far, and the day will not wait for you. Is there anything you need to ask me before you go?"

Where you are: Ostrin Vell's counting-house, at the long counter · Time: Day 1 · morning

Pell leans on the edge of the counter, glances once at the tidy desk, and tells Vell that three questions are all he has before they go. He asks who found Ferr and who has been up the stairs since, what the seal looks like, and whether the lock takes a key or a combination, and whether Ferr's key was taken off the body. He says he won't pay for a broken box. Bram waits until Vell stops tapping, looks at the desk with its pushed-in stool, and asks how big and heavy the box is, who holds the key, and who has been in the room since Ferr died. He remarks that someone tidied the desk before they were sent for, and wants to know who and whether anything was taken.

Vell's mouth tightens at the mention of the stairs. He answers without looking at the desk.

"Wenna Pike keeps the house above Tobin's yard. She found him three mornings back and sent her boy for the Watch. A Watch clerk went up once, the same day, and wrote down that he was dead. Then the physician from the Song of the Morning. Nobody else that I know of. I haven't set foot on those stairs." He pauses. "Wenna has the room key. She has been very clear that she wants her rent."

To Pell he says the wax is dark green, pressed with the scales, his house's mark. "It was whole when the box came to me, and I didn't look at it closer than that." His finger stops on the counter. The box has its own lock, a key and not a combination. Jassan wore the key on a cord at his neck, and the cord went to Wenna with his coat. "Ask her for it."

To Bram he says the box is oak, banded with iron, about the length of his forearm, and heavy. He and the cooper's boy carried it up the week Jassan took the room, and he was sorry for it by the top step. He glances at the desk for the first time and away again. "I didn't touch that desk. Jassan kept it so. Whether Wenna or the Watch straightened it after, I couldn't tell you."

He looks from one of you to the next. "Who knows I sent for it? My clerk is dead. I told no one but the three of you, and the people you're going to ask for keys." He does not say any other name. "Go before the light changes. Bring it here whole."

Where you are: at the counter in Vell's office · Time: Day 1 · morning

Bram said Wenna came first and then the stairs. He told you that you had the kind voice for a landlady wanting her rent, and said that if the key wasn't on the body, Wenna had it. He asked Vell for the Watch clerk's name, and told him to leave the desk as it was and not to move the stool.

Pell asked Vell whether the back wall above Tobin's yard had a window or balcony. He said he would be the one to see Wenna Pike about the key and the cord, while you and Bram kept her busy at the front door. He asked whether Ferr hid things or had a friend who might know where, and warned that whoever carried the box out should not stop to admire the seal, because someone would be watching the door.

Vell answered Pell: a window on the back wall over the yard, a shutter with no glass. The slate wash-house roof runs under it and Tobin's barrels are stacked beneath. No balcony. The stair comes up inside the house to a door on the landing, the only way in he knows. He went up once and didn't stay. To you he said Ferr once mentioned a sister in Nashkel, never named, and that no one but the Watch had come asking. Ferr kept his drawers locked, and Vell never looked in them. The Watch clerk, he told Bram, was young, with a cold, and gave no name. Looking at the stool for the first time, he said he didn't know who tidied that desk, and that it wasn't him.

Pell went out first and the street took him. The Coast Way runs south past the smithies, the ruts still wet from the night's rain. Tobin's yard sits back behind a gate of split oak, barrels stacked along its wall, the smell of wet staves coming over the top.

You and Bram walk up to the front door of the house. The boy on the step gets up and goes in without being asked. A moment later a woman comes out wiping her hands on her apron, a key already in her fist and a cord hanging from it. She looks at the two of you, then at the yard gate, where Pell's back has just passed out of sight behind the barrels.

"You're Vell's," she says. "I was told three." Her eyes go to Bram's shield and stay a moment. "Ferr owed me three gold and four silver, and nobody goes up my stairs till it's paid. Rent first, then the key. That's how I've done it all week, and it hasn't changed for the Watch or for Vell." She holds the key higher, the cord swinging loose. "So. Which of you has the coin?"

Where you are: at the front door of Wenna Pike's house · Time: Day 1 · morning

Bram, beside you, counted out the same sum into Wenna's palm one piece at a time, saying it was Ferr's debt paid by Vell's hired hands and would come off their fee, not the clerk's estate. He then asked who had been up the stairs since the Watch left, anyone with their own key or no business there, and whether anyone had moved the dead man's things before or after the Watch came.

Wenna's hand closes over the coins you hold out. She counts them without looking down, the way a woman counts who has taken rent for years. Bram's hand is still open with silver in it. She glances at it and shakes her head. "One payment's enough. I've had mine." He tips the silver back into his pouch.

"So." She tucks the coins into her apron pocket. "My back's the same, thank you. Tam's my grandson, and he'll be a thief if nobody stops him, so you're right about the quick." She looks at you a moment longer than she needs to, then holds up the key and the cord it hangs from. "Jassan's. The key's for the room door. The little brass one on the cord is for his box, I'd think. He never let it off his neck."

She puts both into your palm and does not let go of the cord until your fingers are round it.

"The Watch boy came first, the morning I found him. The one with the cold in his nose. He went up, wrote in a book on the landing, came down and sneezed into my yard. He took nothing out that I saw, and I stood at the foot of the stair the whole time." She folds her arms. "Then the physician from the Song of the Morning, the second day. Looked, said it was what you'd expect with a man of his build, and went down."

She shifts her weight, and her eyes go past you to the yard gate.

"And a quiet man in a grey coat came round twice. From a counting-house on the Trade Way, he said, though he didn't say which. He wanted to know what was in the room, and he had an open purse and offered me more than the rent for it. I told him to ask the Watch." Her mouth tightens. "He didn't care for that."

To Bram, flatly: "The desk? I never touched his papers. I went up the once, to see him, and came straight down. Whoever put that stool square, it wasn't me." Sefa's eyes go to the clerk's desk and stay there a moment, the capped inkwell, the stool pushed square, before she turns back to Vell.

"Before we go, I have three questions, Master Vell. Who has been into Jassan's room since he died? The landlord, the watch, anyone from this house? A room that's been searched once is easier to take things from than one nobody has touched."

She taps the counter once, where his finger had been.

"Second, the seal. What is pressed into it, and whose wax is it? If we have to swear to you that it arrived whole, I want to know what we are swearing to."

Her voice softens a little. "And third: does anyone else know you've sent for this box? A man who has lost his clerk and a strongbox in one week is a man people come asking after."

Sefa lets Vell finish, then looks at the stool under the clerk's desk, pushed in so square it might have been measured.

"Thank you, Master Vell. One thing more, and then we'll go." She keeps her voice low and even. "You said you told no one but us. I believe you. But you were quick to say it, and a man who is quick to say a thing is often thinking of someone else. Did Jassan have a sister, a friend, a debt-holder who would have asked where he was?"

She turns to Pell and Bram without waiting for the answer. "Wenna Pike wants her rent and has the key. I'll take her. A landlady who has been asked for rent by a stranger all week will talk more readily to a woman who asks after her health and her grandchildren. Pell, the Watch clerk who went up the first day; find out what he wrote down and whether he took anything with him. Bram, go with Pell up to the room if she'll unlock it, and see who else has used those stairs. I'd like the physician's name before we leave the yard, too, if anyone can tell me where the Song of the Morning keeps its healers this week."

She looks at the desk once more, then at Vell. "And Master Vell, if the seal is whole when we bring it, I'd like to see it before it goes in your hands. Not because I doubt you. Because the next person to ask about that box will want to know who looked first."

Sefa steps forward, close enough that Wenna can see she isn't reaching for a weapon, and smiles as if the rent were the most reasonable thing in the world.

"Three gold and four silver. That's fair, and I'll not haggle a landlady over money she's owed." She opens her purse, counts out three gold and four silver into her palm, and holds it out. "I'm paying it from my own purse, mind. Master Vell will settle with me afterward, and I'd rather not argue with him about it today."

She keeps the coins in her hand a moment longer, so Wenna has to look at her to take them.

"How is your back this week, Mistress Pike? The stairs in a house like this must be hard on you. And the little one on the step, is that your grandson? He's a quick one, I could see it from the road."

Her voice stays easy, but she is listening for anything Wenna doesn't say.

"Now, I'll take the key, and the cord with it, since Jassan wore them and his things should go to the people who'll see them rightly used. Before I go up, though, I'd like to know who else has climbed those stairs since the Watch came. Not the clerk, I know about him. Anyone who came asking, or came to take something, or who you've turned away."

Sefa tucks the cord into her palm, the little brass key warm from Wenna's hand, and nods to the old woman as if they had agreed on everything.

"Thank you, Mistress Pike. Your back is in good hands with the boy, I think." She turns to Bram. "Come up with me. Stand at the top of the stairs, where you can see the landing and the street door both. If anyone climbs after us, I want to hear it before they reach the door."

At the top she lifts the door as Wenna told her, and it comes free without a sound. The room is cold and smells of lamp oil and damp wool. A narrow bed is made up square. A table holds an empty cup, a pen, and a stack of paper weighted with a stone. The shutter on the back wall is closed, and a grey thread of light comes around its edge.

Before she goes in, Sefa stops on the landing where the Watch clerk's book lies open on a shelf by the door. She runs one finger down the page without touching the ink, reading the cramped hand.

"'Third day of the month, morning. Jassan Ferr, clerk, found dead in bed. No wound. Face dark, as if from strangling or a fit. Door locked from within. Key with the landlady. Nothing taken that is known.'" She frowns. "Then a second line, added after, in a different ink: 'Strongbox noted, not opened, not removed.' There's no name under it. Only the Watch's stamp, and the stamp is smudged."

She straightens and looks at Bram. "Nothing taken that is known. Someone wrote that line knowing it might be untrue. Keep your eyes on that door."

Then she turns to the room, and her gaze goes straight to the floor by the bed, where the boards are a shade paler in a square the size of a strongbox.

Sefa answers Bram without turning from the bed. "The grey coat wants the box, and he has money to get it. A man who offers more than the rent for a room hasn't finished with the room. He'll come back, and not by the front door." She glances toward the top of the stairs. "And I think someone who wasn't Wenna or the Watch straightened that desk. The tidying was done by someone who knew Jassan kept his papers in order, and knew Vell wouldn't look. Keep your shield where it is. If the stair creaks, call me."

She kneels on the boards beside the bed, careful not to lean her weight on the pale rectangle, and looks at the wax without touching it. The Rune Keeper's gift lets her read what is pressed there. The scales are plain, Vell's house mark. Beside them, smaller and pressed deeper, is a second stamp: a half-moon with a line drawn through it, and under the line, in letters no bigger than a grain of rice, two words in Common. *Paid. Sealed.*

Her breath stops for a moment. She knows the half-moon from nowhere she can name, but she knows what *paid* means on a box that was never Vell's to send. Whoever sealed this strongbox was not a moneylender's clerk. They were telling someone the job was finished.

Sefa does not break the seal. She stays on her knees, takes the candle from her pack, and lights it from the tinderbox, shading the flame with her hand so that the light falls on the wax and nothing else.

"Bram," she says quietly, "come and look at this before you say anything about the box. The seal isn't only Vell's. And I don't think Jassan's landlady was the last person to stand in this room."

Sefa keeps the flame still and looks through the skin of the wax, past the scales and the closed eye, the way she would read a page held up to a window.

"Bram, the box is whole. No scraping on the lock, no pry marks on the oak. The seal is Vell's scales over something else, an eye with its lid drawn down. The wax is moving under the surface, and I don't like it. Don't touch the box yet. I want to see what's under that eye first."

Her voice stays low and steady, though her palms have started to warm.

Whatever lies beneath is too fine and too deep for her to read by one candle. She can feel that it is something made to be read by someone, and that she is not that someone yet.

The warmth in her palms climbs, then settles. The voice does not come again. What comes instead is a simple certainty, like the Lantern's light on a page: this is not a clerk's seal, and it was not meant to be broken by a clerk's hand.

The grey thread of light at the edge of the shutter has widened by a finger's breadth since you came in. Vell said the day would not wait, and it is not waiting.

The strongbox stays where it was pushed, squared to the wall beneath the bed frame. Its iron band is cold, and the lock on its face is a small brass plate with a keyhole, no scratches around it. Your key, warm from Wenna's hand, lies on the cord in your palm.

What does Sefa do?

"Whole," Sefa says, low and steady. "The pressing is sharp. Vell's scales are there, dark green, and there's no ribbon, only the wax itself. Under the scales is the eye, and the eye is pressed deeper than the scales. Nothing's cracked and nothing's lifted."

She keeps her eyes on the wax a moment longer, then looks at the stair gap. "The man in the brown jerkin. Is he watching the front door, or the yard gate? If he's looking at the house, he's looking at the wrong window. Tell me if he moves toward the wash-house wall."

She does not touch the lock. Instead she lays two fingers flat on the iron band nearest her and rocks the box a fraction, testing its weight against the floor. It shifts without a sound. Whatever is inside is heavy, and it sits still.

"I won't open it here," she says. "Vell wants it whole, and so do the people who sealed it. Pell's the one who knows how to get a box down a wall without being seen." She turns toward the shutter, cups one hand beside her mouth, and speaks through the gap in a voice no louder than a draught: "Pell. Back wall. The box is here, and we need a way down that doesn't go past the front door."

Then she looks back at the cord in her palm and the brass key on it, and does not put it to the lock yet.

Beregost wakes to hammers. From every smithy along the street the ringing comes through the shutters of Ostrin Vell's counting-house, where the morning light falls on brass scales and rows of bound ledgers. Pell leans on the counter's edge, eyes going once to the tidy desk and back to Vell.

"Three questions, Master Vell, and then we're off. Who found Ferr, and who's been up those stairs since? A room that's been looked over by the wrong people is a room with the seal half-broken before we reach it. What's the seal like? Wax, ribbon, your own mark? I want to know what whole looks like before I'm the one who has to say it isn't. And the lock. Key or combination? Did Ferr keep his key on him, or did you have to take it off the body?"

He glances at Sefa and Bram before he speaks again. "I'll not be paying for a broken box, Vell."

Pell doesn't look at the desk for long. He's already counting the cooper's yard in his head.

"Good. Now the one that matters to me. Above Tobin's yard, is there a window on the back wall, or a balcony over the barrels? Roofs don't care about the Watch's stairs." He glances at Sefa and Bram, then back at Vell. "I'll go to Wenna Pike for the key and the cord. You two can keep her talking at the front door, and I'll see what the room looks like before anyone's feet go in. Anyone who went up there before us will have left some sign, and I'd rather find it than be told about it."

He leans in a little, voice dropping. "And Master Vell, if Ferr kept a ledger he didn't want the Watch reading, he'd have kept it close. Did he have a habit of hiding things, or a friend who might know where?"

He straightens, hand already on the counter's edge ready to go. "Also, the moment you're carrying that box out of here, don't stop to admire the seal. Somebody will be watching the door."

Pell keeps moving until the barrels are between him and the gate, then stops and sets his back against the wet staves.

"Chalk ring with a notch," he murmurs, low enough that only the wall could hear. "That's a Guild eye, not a Watch one. Someone's paid to see who comes and goes from Wenna's stairs. Good. Then they'll be looking at the front door, not the yard."

He turns his head slowly, reading the lane through the gap between two barrels. He looks for a man leaning on a wall with nothing to do, a boy with a loaf who doesn't eat it, a cart that stays put too long.

"Tobin's barrels are a ladder, if nobody's counting. Three stacks, the middle one's taller." He is already measuring the top with his eyes. "I'm going up. If anyone asks, I'm a yard boy who lost a cooper's hoop."

He climbs the barrel stack quietly, staves creaking under his boots, and gets a hand on the top of the wall. Once he's over, he drops flat against the slate of the wash-house roof and crawls along it toward the back wall of the house, eyes on the shutter with no glass.

"Keep Wenna talking, Sefa," he breathes toward the street, not loud enough to carry. "I want the window before the door."

Pell lies still on the slate for a breath, then reaches for the sill without letting his weight shift the tiles.

"Someone's been in," he says under his breath, and it is not a question. He thumbs the pale scrape, then sights along the bar from the side, mouth tight. "Thin blade, worked under and lifted. Not a Watch man's crowbar. Someone who knew how to open a shutter without leaving a mess." He leans closer, eyes on the iron keeper. "Lifted once, set back. Sloppy with the wood, neat with the bar. Could be the same hand that sent the watcher to the cart, or just somebody who came before us and didn't want the landlady to know."

He draws his dagger slowly, not to use it, just to hold the point of it under the bar and test the lift without moving the latch. "I'm not going through the shutter yet. The bar's been set, so whoever lifted it set it for a reason. I'll see if it moves for me the same way before I put my weight on it."

He glances down at the yard, then toward the street where Sefa's voice would be, though he can't hear it from here. "Sefa, Wenna's door. I've got a window that's been opened by someone who isn't Wenna. Tell me what she says about the stairs."

Pell waits a breath longer, watching the watcher's back at the lane's end, then sets the dagger's point under the bar again.

"Sefa's at the door, and that man's got his eyes on her, not on the roof," he murmurs. "I'm going in now, while the stairs are still a long way off."

He lifts the bar the way it was lifted before, one finger's width, and slides the shutter back just enough to fit his body through. He drops feet first onto the boards inside, crouches under the sill, and waits for the house to answer. Nothing but the drip of the wash-house gutter outside.

Before he stands, his eyes go over the floor: the dust by the door, the bed, the oak box with its iron bands. He keeps his boots off the one clean stretch in front of the box. Then he looks for the drawers Vell mentioned, locked, and for anyone else's tracks in the grey dust.

"Two sets of boot-marks on the floor," he whispers to himself. "One fresh, one older. The fresh one stops at the box and turns back."
[Roll the die]

The grey dust has kept a clear record. Three days of undisturbed dust lie over most of the floor, and the older marks are Jassan's own: a clerk's plain soft shoes, worn at the heel, going from the bed to the desk and back a hundred times, with a patch where he always stood.

Over those marks run newer ones. A heavier boot, a man's by the size of it, with a square toe and a nail missing from the sole. These prints are sharp at the edges, and the dust has not yet filled them in. They come in from the door and go straight to the oak box. The dust around it is pressed in two places, where a man knelt and then pushed back on his heels. Then the prints turn and go to the desk. Here they wander. The drawers have been tried: a fingernail's worth of scoring around the lock of the lowest one, and a pale wedge of wood where something was levered and slipped. After that the prints go back to the door and out onto the landing.

There is a third mark, close to the bed, that you can't put a foot to: a long smear in the dust, as if a sack or a bundle had been dragged a short way and then lifted.

The box itself has no marks on its lid. The wax seal on its clasp is whole, dark green, pressed with the scales. Nobody has broken it.

From the landing, very faintly, you hear the house stir: a door, feet on the stairs, a woman's voice raised in the street. The sound is Sefa's, speaking to Wenna Pike, and it is coming up the stairwell toward the room.
[Onward]

Pell freezes at the sound of Sefa's voice on the stairs, then sees that the print under the shutter is his own. He notes it and keeps still.

"That's mine," he breathes, and hooks a boot toe over the edge of the sill so no more dust gets stirred. "The narrow ones with no nails, from the door to the bed and back. Those are the ones I want."

He keeps to the far side of the old marks, moving only as far as the box, and looks at the oak lid without touching it. The green wax is whole, the scales pressed sharp. He does not lift the box, only tilts his head to see the clasp and the lock plate. A key, as Vell said, and no scratches around it.

"Lock's not been worked," he murmurs. "Whoever came first didn't want the box. They wanted the drawers."

He eases toward the desk, keeping his boots out of the clean rectangle beside the bed, and looks at the drawer where a wedge of pale wood shows. He does not try the lock. Downstairs, Wenna's voice rises, and Sefa's answers, calm and soft.

"Sefa's bringing her up," he says, quieter. "Bram, if you're listening through that door, stand where the landing light doesn't reach the box. I want to be behind the bed when that latch goes."

Pell eases back along the far wall, away from the clean rectangle, and slides in behind the narrow bed where the shadow is deepest. He crouches low, one hand flat on the boards, the other resting on the hilt of his shortsword.

"Stairs first, then the latch," he breathes toward the door. "Sefa, keep her in the doorway. Don't let her walk past the box. If she's seen the box, she'll wonder why we're looking at the drawers."

He glances once at the desk, at the pale wedge in the wood beside the lock, and files it away. Nothing else will be touched until the landlady has said her piece.

"Bram, when the door opens, you stay where the light doesn't reach. I'll be out of her eye by the bed." He pauses, listening to Wenna's voice climb the last steps. "And if she asks who's been up here before us, let her say it first. Landladies always know more than they mean to tell."

Overall I enjoyed it. Pell's choices had visible consequences, the world felt like it had its own business (the watcher, the drawers someone had already tried), and the other two characters had clear hooks for their next turns.
